newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore MP frets teen violence may turn racial.
newsitem.headline: Singapore MP frets teen violence may turn racial.

text.p: Rising teenage violence in Singapore could become a serious problem if the young gang up along racial lines, a ruling party member of parliament said on Thursday.
"The issue of youth gangs and violence will be lost sight of in the larger racial tension which will follow," Davinder Singh told parliament.
"There will be distrust and all sorts of suspicions between neighbours of different races. That will be a tragedy."
Singapore handles the issue of race, language, religion and culture with extreme sensitivity following bloody racial riots more than three decades ago.
Ethnic Chinese form 77.7 percent of Singapore's three million population. Malays form 14.1 percent, Indians 7.1 percent and 1.1 percent are of other races such as Eurasians and Arabs.

Ho Peng Kee, Minister of State for Home Affairs, told parliament that even though fights between teenage gangs of different races rose to 27 in 1996 from 11 in 1993, they were a relatively minor problem in relation to overall teenage gang violence.
Fights between different racial groups last year comprised only 12 percent of violent teenage incidents, he said.
Ho said while juvenile delinquency cases dropped to 2,101 last year from 2,574 in 1995, teenage gang fights had risen and more would be done to tackle the problem.
According to media reports, police have recorded 148 violent incidents involving teenagers so far this year, up from 105 for the same period last year.
The government has increasingly highlighted the growing problem of teenage violence and teenage gangs over the past few months.
The problem is seen as denting Signapore's image as one of the world's safest places because of its strict laws and stiff punishments.
Seven MPs spoke on the issue in parliament, asking for a variety of steps to be taken to control the problem such as the formation of an inter-ministerial task force.

Singapore has recently taken several steps to curb teenage violence, the latest being a ban on teenagers under 16 years from attending "tea" or afternoon dances at discos which are considered the breeding ground for teenage gangs.

But MPs were divided on the best action to take with some saying barring on teenagers from discos or billiard halls would force them to go "underground" for entertainment and would not solve the root of the problem.
